A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same piano-roll diffusion guidance framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing content to be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original POP909 accompaniment-generation results against WholeSongGen and GETMusic in Table 1, alongside generated examples in Figure 4.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, chord-only generation, guidance-weight experiments, and a 31-participant listening study in Tables 1–4, Figure 3, and the appendices.

M1.justification: FTG is renamed FGG, but the conditional diffusion model, classifier-free guidance objective, intermediate noise projection, rhythmic constraints, and DDIM adaptation remain. The conditioning equations move into Appendix B; neither that relocation nor the additional experiments establishes a new method component.

E1.justification: POP909 and melody/chord-conditioned accompaniment remain the principal coverage. V2 adds chord-only music generation in Appendix D.3, changing the required conditioning inputs. Section 5.2 also newly reports generation examples using Dorian and Chinese pentatonic scales.

E2.justification: WholeSongGen and GETMusic remain the main accompaniment comparators. V2 adds rule-based editing after sampling as an evaluated alternative in Table 2, alongside training-only and uncontrolled variants. The new chord-only comparison reuses GETMusic rather than introducing another external baseline.

E3.justification: Reported training changes from 10 epochs of 985 steps to 12-key augmentation yielding 189,132 samples and 23,642 iterations. V2 also introduces an out-of-key-step metric, ablation and guidance-weight protocols, and randomized, source-blinded listening ratings from 31 participants. The POP909 split and backbone remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 primarily illustrates note replacement qualitatively. V2 retains those examples in Appendix F and adds quantitative tests separating training conditioning, sampling control, post-sampling editing, and no control. Appendix G additionally varies guidance weight from 0.5 to 10 to examine rhythmic adherence and output degradation.

E5.justification: Both versions already report 95% confidence intervals for objective scores. V2 newly specifies matched random seeds across ablation conditions and reports confidence intervals for listener ratings. It does not establish an increased number of independent training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the proposed method's chord/pitch/duration/density scores of 0.715/0.579/0.548/0.714 with 0.767/0.628/0.595/0.843; baseline scores remain unchanged, changing the duration and density rankings. These results accompany revised training settings. V2 also adds out-of-key frequencies, ablation, chord-only, listening-study, and guidance-weight results.

T1.justification: The minimax lower-bound argument changes substantially: v1 Appendix C.1's Property I, Property II, and estimator assumption are removed, and v2 Appendix A.3 substitutes a restricted-total-variation argument with a normalized distribution class. The lower-bound rate and the separate KL-divergence bounds remain, despite renumbering and relocation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains precise harmonic/rhythmic guidance with theoretical and empirical support for interactive generation. V2 additionally claims adaptation to tonal frameworks absent from training and positions its demo among the first enabling real-time interaction. Its abstract emphasizes composer intent and listenability more explicitly.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation: it applies the KL discussion to unseen tonal frameworks, explains advantages over post-sampling editing, interprets guidance-weight tradeoffs, and argues that feature overlap is unsuitable for chord-only evaluation. It also recasts the precision argument around tonic-centric genres and softens v1's categorical statement about inability to reproduce compositional artistry.

D1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds explicit transposition, chord-adjustment, and sampling-without-replacement instructions, while Appendix E supplies participant characteristics and the listening questionnaire. Existing piano-roll channel construction, backbone description, optimizer and diffusion parameters, GPU timing, and demo access remain largely unchanged or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Rombach et al. (2022), Chang et al. (2023), Gao et al. (2023), and Lin et al. (2024), while removing the ControlNet citation to Zhang et al. (2023b). Detailed positioning against reflected diffusion and non-differentiable rule-guided diffusion is retained.

P1.justification: The introduction and motivation are extensively rewritten, methodology now precedes the statistical challenge discussion, and conditioning and training details move into reorganized appendices. Experiments are reordered and a conclusion is added. The title, terminology, and author list also change.

P2.justification: V1 Figure 3 is split and enlarged into v2 Figures 1–2. Existing projection and note-replacement illustrations are relocated, while the notation table and several motivational score examples disappear. V2 adds listening and participant plots, three experimental tables, and an out-of-key column in Table 1.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical diagnosis through component ablations, guidance-weight analysis, and listener ratings absent from v1. However, its revised lower-bound proof removes estimator assumptions and introduces an unsupported equality in Equation 31. The new unseen-mode interpretation also invokes a KL proof assuming ground-truth support inside the constraint set. Finally, the listening-study overview describes ground-truth accompaniments whereas Appendix E.2 describes melody-only reference clips. These gains and reliability concerns prevent a confident net-quality judgment.
